title: Domains & DNS
summary: Understand how names on the internet work: buy a domain, master DNS records and TTLs, connect it to hosting, add free HTTPS, and set up email records that keep you out of spam.

lessons.title: What a domain name is
lessons.summary: Understand domain names as human-friendly names for IP addresses.

slides.title: Computers use numbers
slides.text:
Every server on the internet has an **IP address**:

- IPv4: `93.184.215.14`
- IPv6: `2606:2800:21f:cb07:6820:80da:af6b:8b2c`

Hard to remember!
slides.narration: Computers on the internet find each other by IP address, a number like ninety three dot one eight four and so on, or a much longer IPv6 address. People are bad at remembering numbers like these.

slides.title: Names for humans
slides.text:
A **domain name** is a readable name that points to those numbers:

`example.com` -> `93.184.215.14`

The system that translates is **DNS**, the Domain Name System.
slides.narration: A domain name is a human friendly name, like example dot com, that points to those numbers. The Domain Name System, or DNS, is the global phone book that translates names into addresses.

slides.title: Reading a domain right to left
slides.text:
`blog.shop.example.co.uk.`

- `.` root (usually hidden)
- `uk` top-level domain
- `co.uk` public suffix
- `example.co.uk` the registered domain
- `shop`, `blog` subdomains
slides.narration: Domains are read from right to left, from general to specific. At the very end is an invisible dot, the root. Then comes the top level domain, like u k. Then the name someone registered, and on the left any subdomains the owner created.

slides.title: Domain vs URL
slides.text:
`https://blog.example.com:443/posts/1?ref=x`

- scheme: `https`
- **host (domain)**: `blog.example.com`
- port: `443`
- path: `/posts/1`
- query: `?ref=x`
slides.narration: A domain is only one part of a web address. A full URL also includes the scheme like https, sometimes a port, a path to a page, and a query string. DNS only cares about the host name part.

slides.title: You rent, not own
slides.text:
- You **register** a domain for 1-10 years
- You must renew it, or it expires and someone else can take it
- Turn on **auto-renew**!
slides.narration: One important detail: you never truly own a domain, you rent it. You register it for one to ten years and must renew it. If it expires, someone else can grab it, so always turn on auto renew for domains that matter.

lessons.notes:
## IP addresses

Every device reachable on the internet has an **IP address**:
- **IPv4**: four numbers 0-255, e.g. `203.0.113.10` (about 4.3 billion addresses, effectively exhausted).
- **IPv6**: eight groups of hex, e.g. `2001:db8::1` (enormous space; adoption keeps growing).

## Domain names

A **domain name** is a human-readable label mapped to IP addresses (and other data) by **DNS**. DNS is distributed: no single server knows everything.

## Structure

Domains form a tree, read **right to left**:

```
.                    root
com.                 top-level domain (TLD)
example.com.         second-level domain (what you register)
www.example.com.     subdomain (you create it for free)
```

The trailing dot means "fully qualified"; browsers hide it.

Some countries use a second level for registration, like `co.uk` or `com.au`. The list of these "public suffixes" is maintained in the **Public Suffix List**.

## Domain vs URL

```
https://shop.example.com/cart?id=7
\___/   \______________/\___/\___/
scheme      host        path query
```

## Rules for names

- Letters, digits and hyphens; not starting or ending with a hyphen.
- Each label up to 63 characters; full name up to 253.
- Case-insensitive: `Example.COM` = `example.com`.
- International names (like `cafe` with an accent) are stored as **Punycode** (`xn--...`).

## Renting

You **register** a domain through a registrar for a period (1-10 years) and renew it. Expired domains go through grace and redemption periods and then may be released to the public.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Translates domain names into IP addresses and other records
quiz.explain: DNS is the internet phone book.

quiz.q: In `blog.example.com`, which part is the TLD?
quiz.explain: The top-level domain is the rightmost label.

quiz.q: What happens if you forget to renew your domain?
options: It eventually expires and someone else can register it
quiz.explain: After grace periods, expired domains can be released.

lessons.task: Open a terminal and run `nslookup example.com` (Windows, macOS, Linux) or `dig example.com` (macOS/Linux). Write down the IP addresses you get. Then split three URLs you use daily into scheme, host, path and query.

lessons.title: Top-level domains (TLDs)
lessons.summary: Explore the kinds of TLDs and how to pick one.

slides.title: Kinds of TLDs
slides.text:
- **gTLD** generic: `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, `.info`
- **ccTLD** country code: `.uk`, `.de`, `.bd`, `.jp`
- **new gTLDs**: `.dev`, `.app`, `.shop`, `.blog`
- **sponsored / restricted**: `.gov`, `.edu`, `.mil`
slides.narration: Top level domains come in a few kinds. Generic ones like dot com and dot org are open to everyone. Country code domains are two letters, like dot u k or dot b d. Since twenty fourteen hundreds of new generic ones appeared, like dot dev and dot shop. Some, like dot gov, are restricted.

slides.title: Who runs them
slides.text:
- **ICANN** coordinates the root and TLD policy
- Each TLD has a **registry** (e.g. Verisign runs `.com`)
- **Registrars** sell names to you
slides.narration: ICANN coordinates the whole system and approves top level domains. Each TLD is run by a registry, for example Verisign runs dot com. You buy names from a registrar, which talks to the registry for you.

slides.title: Hacked ccTLDs
slides.text:
Some country codes are used like generic TLDs:
- `.io` (British Indian Ocean Territory)
- `.ai` (Anguilla)
- `.co` (Colombia), `.me` (Montenegro), `.tv` (Tuvalu)

Rules and prices are set by that country.
slides.narration: Some country codes became popular for other reasons. Dot i o is loved by tech companies, and dot a i by artificial intelligence startups. Remember they still belong to a country, which sets the rules and prices and could change them.

slides.title: Special TLDs
slides.text:
- `.dev` and `.app`: **HTTPS required** (HSTS preloaded)
- `.test`, `.example`, `.invalid`, `.localhost`: reserved, never real
- `.local`: used by mDNS on local networks
- `.internal`: reserved for private networks
slides.narration: Some TLDs have special behavior. Dot dev and dot app force HTTPS in every browser. Dot test, dot example and dot localhost are reserved and will never exist on the public internet, which makes them perfect for testing. Dot internal is reserved for private networks.

slides.title: Choosing a TLD
slides.text:
- `.com` is still the most trusted and remembered
- Local business? Your **ccTLD**
- Check renewal price, not just the first-year price
- Avoid TLDs often abused for spam
slides.narration: When choosing, dot com is still the most familiar. For a local business, your country code builds trust. Always check the renewal price, because cheap first years can hide expensive renewals, and avoid TLDs with a reputation for spam.

lessons.notes:
## The top of the tree

A **top-level domain (TLD)** is the last label of a domain. There are over 1,400 TLDs in the root zone.

## Categories

| Type | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Generic (gTLD) | `.com`, `.net`, `.org` | open to anyone |
| Country code (ccTLD) | `.uk`, `.de`, `.in`, `.bd`, `.jp` | two letters, rules set by each country |
| New gTLDs | `.dev`, `.app`, `.shop`, `.xyz`, `.blog` | added from 2013 onwards |
| Sponsored/restricted | `.gov`, `.edu`, `.mil`, `.museum` | eligibility required |
| Brand TLDs | `.google`, `.bmw` | owned by companies |

ICANN opened its **next round** of new gTLD applications in 2026, so more TLDs will appear in the coming years.

## The players

- **ICANN** - coordinates names and numbers, accredits registrars.
- **IANA** - manages the root zone.
- **Registry** - operates one TLD (Verisign: `.com`/`.net`; Google Registry: `.dev`/`.app`; Nominet: `.uk`).
- **Registrar** - sells registrations to the public.

## Special-use names

- `.test`, `.example`, `.invalid`, `.localhost` - reserved by RFC 2606/6761; safe for docs and testing.
- `.local` - multicast DNS on your LAN (e.g. `printer.local`).
- `.internal` - reserved in 2024 for private use inside organizations.
- `.dev`, `.app`, `.page` - on the **HSTS preload list**: browsers only load them over HTTPS.

## Choosing well

1. Easy to say and spell.
2. Matches your audience (global: `.com`; local: your ccTLD).
3. Compare **renewal** prices.
4. Register common typos or your name in other key TLDs if your brand matters.

quiz.q: Which is a country-code TLD?
quiz.explain: .de is Germany's two-letter country code.

quiz.q: What is special about `.dev`?
quiz.explain: .dev is on the HSTS preload list, so HTTPS is mandatory.

quiz.q: Which TLD is reserved for testing and will never be real?
quiz.explain: .test is reserved by RFC 2606.

lessons.task: Brainstorm a name for a project. Check its availability in three TLDs at a registrar (just search, do not buy). Compare first-year and renewal prices in a small table and pick one with a reason.

lessons.title: Registrars and buying a domain
lessons.summary: Buy a domain safely, understand WHOIS and protect it from theft.

slides.title: Where to buy
slides.text:
Accredited **registrars**, for example:
- Cloudflare Registrar (at-cost)
- Porkbun, Namecheap
- Squarespace Domains, GoDaddy
- Your hosting company

Prices for `.com`: roughly $10-12/year.
slides.narration: You buy a domain from an accredited registrar. Popular choices include Cloudflare, which sells at cost, Porkbun and Namecheap. A dot com usually costs around ten to twelve dollars a year. Be careful with add-ons you do not need.

slides.title: The buying steps
slides.text:
1. Search the name
2. Pick the years and **auto-renew**
3. Enter real contact details (required)
4. Enable privacy / redaction
5. Pay and verify your email
slides.narration: Buying is simple. Search the name, choose how many years, and turn on auto renew. Enter real contact details, because the registrar is required to have them, and keep them private. Finally, pay and confirm your email address, or the domain may be suspended.

slides.title: WHOIS and RDAP
slides.text:
- Public lookup of domain registration data
- Shows registrar, dates, name servers, status
- Personal data is mostly **redacted** (GDPR)
- RDAP is the modern JSON replacement for WHOIS
slides.narration: Anyone can look up a domain registration using WHOIS or its modern replacement, RDAP. You will see the registrar, the creation and expiry dates and the name servers. Personal contact details are usually hidden for privacy.

slides.title: Protect your domain
slides.text:
- Strong password + **2FA** on the registrar account
- Auto-renew + valid payment card
- **Registrar lock** (transfer lock) on
- Use an email that is NOT on the same domain
slides.narration: Your domain is a key to your whole online presence, so protect it. Use a strong password and two factor authentication. Keep auto renew on with a valid card, and turn on the transfer lock. Use a recovery email on a different domain, so you are not locked out if the domain breaks.

slides.title: Transfers
slides.text:
- Move to another registrar with an **auth code** (EPP code)
- Not allowed within 60 days of registration or a previous transfer
- Usually adds one year to the expiry
slides.narration: You can move a domain to another registrar. Unlock it, get the authorization code, and start the transfer at the new registrar. Transfers are blocked for sixty days after registration, and a transfer usually adds a year to your registration.

lessons.notes:
## Registrars

A **registrar** is a company accredited by ICANN (or by a ccTLD registry) to register domains for customers. Examples: Cloudflare Registrar, Porkbun, Namecheap, Squarespace Domains (which took over Google Domains), GoDaddy, Gandi, and many hosting providers.

## Steps to buy

1. Search availability.
2. Choose the term (1-10 years) and **enable auto-renew**.
3. Provide accurate contact data (required by ICANN; false data can lead to suspension).
4. Enable WHOIS privacy / redaction (often free).
5. Pay and **verify your email** within the deadline.

## Costs

- Standard `.com`: about $10-12/year at good registrars.
- Some TLDs are much more expensive (`.io`, `.ai` often $50-100+/year).
- **Premium** names can cost hundreds or thousands.
- Watch out for upsells (hosting bundles, "SEO", email) and high renewal prices.

## WHOIS / RDAP

```bash
whois example.com
# or open https://lookup.icann.org
```

Since 2025, ICANN no longer requires gTLD registries and registrars to run the old WHOIS service; **RDAP** is the official replacement.

## Domain statuses

- `clientTransferProhibited` - registrar lock is on (good).
- `pendingDelete`, `redemptionPeriod` - expiring; act fast.

## Security checklist

- 2FA on the registrar account (prefer an authenticator app or passkey).
- Registrar lock on.
- Auto-renew on and a valid card.
- Recovery email on another domain.
- For high-value domains: **registry lock** (manual verification for changes).

## Transfers

Unlock the domain, request the **auth/EPP code**, start the transfer at the new registrar, approve the confirmation email. A 60-day lock applies after registration or transfer.

quiz.q: What is a registrar?
options: The company that runs a whole TLD
An accredited company that sells domain registrations
quiz.explain: Registrars sell names; registries run TLDs.

quiz.q: Which setting prevents someone moving your domain to another registrar without you?
quiz.explain: The transfer lock blocks unauthorized transfers.

quiz.q: Why use a recovery email that is not on the same domain?
options: If the domain breaks or expires you can still receive account emails
quiz.explain: Otherwise a domain problem could lock you out of fixing it.

lessons.task: Look up three domains with https://lookup.icann.org (or `whois`). For each, note the registrar, creation date, expiry date, name servers and status codes.

lessons.title: How DNS resolution works, step by step
lessons.summary: Follow a DNS lookup from your browser to the authoritative server and back.

slides.title: The question
slides.text:
You type `www.example.com`.

Your computer needs its **IP address** before it can connect.

Who does it ask?
slides.narration: You type www dot example dot com into your browser. Before anything can load, your computer needs the IP address. Let us follow the question step by step.

slides.title: Step 1: local caches
slides.text:
1. Browser cache
2. Operating system cache
3. `hosts` file

Found? Done. Otherwise ask the **recursive resolver**.
slides.narration: First your computer checks its own memory. The browser has a cache, the operating system has a cache, and there is a hosts file. If the answer is there, it is used instantly. If not, the question goes to a recursive resolver.

slides.title: Step 2: the recursive resolver
slides.text:
Usually run by your ISP, or public ones:
- Cloudflare `1.1.1.1`
- Google `8.8.8.8`
- Quad9 `9.9.9.9`

It does the hard work and caches answers.
slides.narration: The recursive resolver is a server that does the searching for you. It is usually run by your internet provider, or you can use a public one like Cloudflare one dot one dot one dot one, or Google eight dot eight dot eight dot eight. It also caches answers for everyone using it.

slides.title: Step 3: walking the tree
slides.text:
1. Ask a **root server**: "who knows `.com`?"
2. Ask the **`.com` TLD server**: "who knows `example.com`?"
3. Ask the **authoritative server** for `example.com`: "what is `www`?"
4. Get the answer: `93.184.215.14`
slides.narration: If the resolver has nothing cached, it walks down the tree. It asks a root server, which points to the dot com servers. The dot com servers point to the name servers for example dot com. Those authoritative servers give the final answer.

slides.title: Step 4: answer and cache
slides.text:
Resolver returns the IP to your computer and **caches** it for the record's **TTL**.

Next person asking gets it instantly.
slides.narration: The resolver sends the address back to your computer, and both store it for a time called the TTL. The next lookup for the same name is answered straight from cache, which is why DNS is fast.

slides.title: Try it yourself
slides.text: See every step:
slides.narration: You can watch this happen. The dig command with plus trace shows each step from the root down. On Windows, nslookup gives you the final answer, and you can choose which resolver to ask.
slides.code:
dig +trace www.example.com

# Windows / any OS
nslookup www.example.com
nslookup www.example.com 1.1.1.1

lessons.notes:
## The players

| Role | Job |
|---|---|
| **Stub resolver** | the small DNS client in your OS |
| **Recursive resolver** | finds answers for clients, caches them (ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9) |
| **Root servers** | 13 named server sets (a. to m.root-servers.net), hundreds of anycast instances worldwide |
| **TLD servers** | know the name servers for every domain in a TLD |
| **Authoritative servers** | hold the actual records for a domain |

## A full lookup for `www.example.com`

1. Browser and OS caches are checked, plus the `hosts` file.
2. The OS asks the configured **recursive resolver**.
3. Resolver (cold cache) asks a **root server** -> referral to `.com` servers.
4. Resolver asks a **`.com` server** -> referral to `example.com`'s name servers (NS records).
5. Resolver asks the **authoritative server** -> answer: `A 93.184.215.14`.
6. Resolver caches the answer for its **TTL** and returns it.
7. Browser connects to the IP.

Most lookups skip steps 3-5 because the answers are already cached.

## Tools

```bash
dig www.example.com            # ask your resolver
dig +trace www.example.com     # walk from the root yourself
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com MX    # ask a specific resolver for MX records
nslookup www.example.com       # works on Windows too
```

## Privacy and security

- Classic DNS is **unencrypted UDP on port 53**.
- **DoH** (DNS over HTTPS) and **DoT** (DNS over TLS) encrypt queries; modern browsers and OSes support them.
- **DNSSEC** adds signatures so resolvers can check answers were not forged. It protects integrity, not privacy.

## Why "it works for me but not for you"

Different resolvers may have cached different answers. Until the old TTL expires, some users see old data. This is often called "DNS propagation".

quiz.q: Which server holds the actual records for a domain?
quiz.explain: Authoritative servers give the final answer.

quiz.q: What does the recursive resolver do?
options: Finds the answer on behalf of the client and caches it
quiz.explain: It walks the DNS tree and caches results.

quiz.q: What is the order a resolver follows with an empty cache?
quiz.explain: It starts at the root and works down.

lessons.task: Run `nslookup` (or `dig`) for three websites using your default resolver and then using `1.1.1.1`. If you have `dig`, run `dig +trace` on one site and label which lines come from the root, the TLD and the authoritative servers.

lessons.title: DNS record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS
lessons.summary: Learn the most important DNS records and what each is used for.

slides.title: A zone file
slides.text: A domain's records live in its **zone**:
slides.narration: All the DNS records for a domain live in its zone. Each record has a name, a time to live, a type and a value. Let us look at the most common types one by one.
slides.code:
; name    TTL   type   value
@        3600  A      203.0.113.10
@        3600  AAAA   2001:db8::10
www      3600  CNAME  example.com.
@        3600  MX     10 mail.example.com.
@        3600  TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
@        86400 NS     ns1.dnsprovider.com.

slides.title: A and AAAA
slides.text:
- **A** -> IPv4 address: `203.0.113.10`
- **AAAA** -> IPv6 address: `2001:db8::10`

You can have several for load sharing.
slides.narration: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. A quad A record maps it to an IPv6 address. A name can have several of each, and resolvers will share traffic among them.

slides.title: CNAME
slides.text:
**Alias** to another name:

`www  CNAME  myapp.netlify.app.`

- Cannot sit at the root (`@`) of a domain
- Cannot coexist with other records on the same name
- Some providers offer **ALIAS / ANAME / CNAME flattening** for the root
slides.narration: A CNAME record says this name is an alias for another name. It is great for pointing www to a hosting platform. But a CNAME cannot be used at the bare root of a domain, and it cannot share its name with other records. Many DNS providers offer flattening or ALIAS records to solve the root problem.

slides.title: MX
slides.text:
**Mail exchanger**: where email for the domain goes.

`@ MX 10 mx1.mail.com.`
`@ MX 20 mx2.mail.com.`

Lower number = higher priority.
slides.narration: MX records tell other mail servers where to deliver email for your domain. Each has a priority number, and lower numbers are tried first. The value must be a host name, never an IP address.

slides.title: TXT
slides.text:
Free text used for **verification and policies**:
- domain ownership checks (Google, Microsoft, GitHub)
- **SPF**, **DKIM**, **DMARC** email records
- certificate validation (`_acme-challenge`)
slides.narration: TXT records hold text. They are used to prove you own a domain to services like Google or GitHub, and for email security policies such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC. They also help certificate authorities verify you.

slides.title: NS and others
slides.text:
- **NS**: which servers are authoritative for the zone
- **SOA**: zone admin info and serial number
- **CAA**: which CAs may issue certificates
- **SRV**: service host and port
- **PTR**: reverse lookup (IP -> name)
- **HTTPS/SVCB**: modern connection hints
slides.narration: NS records list the authoritative name servers for a zone. There are also others you will meet: SOA with admin information, CAA which limits who can issue certificates, SRV for services, PTR for reverse lookups, and the newer HTTPS record that helps browsers connect faster.

lessons.notes:
## Record anatomy

Every record has: **name**, **TTL**, **class** (almost always `IN`), **type**, **value**. `@` means the zone root (e.g. `example.com`).

## The essential types

| Type | Value | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | IPv4 address | `@ A 203.0.113.10` |
| **AAAA** | IPv6 address | `@ AAAA 2001:db8::10` |
| **CNAME** | another host name | `www CNAME example.com.` |
| **MX** | priority + mail host | `@ MX 10 mx.example.net.` |
| **TXT** | text | SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification |
| **NS** | name server | `@ NS ns1.provider.net.` |

## CNAME rules

- A CNAME **cannot** be at the zone apex (`@`), because the apex must have SOA and NS records, and a CNAME cannot coexist with other records.
- Solutions for the apex: an A/AAAA record, or provider features called **ALIAS**, **ANAME** or **CNAME flattening** (Cloudflare, Route 53 alias, DNSimple...).
- Do not chain many CNAMEs: each one adds a lookup.

## MX tips

- Values must be **host names**, not IPs, and must not point to a CNAME.
- Lower preference number = tried first. Equal numbers share load.

## More records you will meet

- **SOA** - start of authority: primary server, admin, serial, timers.
- **CAA** - `@ CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` limits which CAs may issue certificates.
- **SRV** - `_sip._tcp` service with priority, weight, port, target.
- **PTR** - reverse DNS (IP to name), set by whoever owns the IP (your host).
- **HTTPS / SVCB** - tell browsers about HTTP/3 support and other hints before connecting.

## Query them

```bash
dig example.com A +short
dig example.com AAAA +short
dig www.github.com CNAME +short
dig gmail.com MX +short
dig example.com TXT +short
dig example.com NS +short
```

quiz.q: Which record maps a name to an IPv6 address?
quiz.explain: AAAA (quad-A) holds IPv6 addresses.

quiz.q: Why can you not put a plain CNAME at the root (`@`) of a domain?
options: The apex needs SOA/NS records and a CNAME cannot coexist with other records
quiz.explain: Use A/AAAA or ALIAS/flattening at the apex instead.

quiz.q: Two MX records have priorities 10 and 20. Which is tried first?
quiz.explain: Lower number means higher priority.

lessons.task: Use `nslookup -type=MX gmail.com`, `nslookup -type=TXT google.com` and `nslookup -type=NS wikipedia.org` (or the `dig` equivalents). Write down what each record means in plain English.

lessons.title: TTL and DNS propagation
lessons.summary: Control how long DNS answers are cached and plan changes without surprises.

slides.title: What is TTL?
slides.text:
**Time To Live**: how many seconds a resolver may cache a record.

- `300` = 5 minutes
- `3600` = 1 hour
- `86400` = 1 day
slides.narration: Every DNS record has a time to live, measured in seconds. It tells resolvers how long they may keep the answer in their cache before asking again. Three hundred is five minutes, thirty six hundred is one hour.

slides.title: The trade-off
slides.text:
- **Long TTL**: fewer lookups, faster for users, resilient if DNS is down; but changes are slow
- **Short TTL**: changes spread fast; more queries
slides.narration: There is a trade-off. A long TTL means fewer lookups and slightly faster sites, but any change takes a long time to reach everyone. A short TTL means changes spread fast, but resolvers have to ask more often.

slides.title: "Propagation" is really caching
slides.text:
DNS changes are instant on your server.

Old answers live on in caches until their **old TTL** runs out.

That is why some people see the new site and some the old one.
slides.narration: People often talk about DNS propagation, as if changes slowly travel around the world. In reality the change is instant on your DNS server. The delay comes from caches holding the old answer until its TTL expires.

slides.title: Plan a migration
slides.text:
1. A day before: lower TTL to 300
2. Wait for the **old** TTL to expire
3. Change the record
4. Verify; keep the old server running a while
5. Raise TTL back (e.g. 3600)
slides.narration: To move a site with almost no delay, lower the TTL to five minutes a day before. Wait for the old TTL to expire, then make the change. Most users switch within minutes. Keep the old server running for a while, and afterwards raise the TTL again.

slides.title: Check the TTL
slides.text: The number after the name is the remaining TTL:
slides.narration: With dig you can see the TTL. Ask your resolver twice and you will see the number counting down, because it is the remaining time in the cache. Asking the authoritative server directly shows the full configured value.
slides.code:
dig example.com A
;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.   2475   IN   A   93.184.215.14

# ask the authoritative server directly
dig @ns1.example-dns.com example.com A

lessons.notes:
## Time To Live

The **TTL** of a record is the number of seconds resolvers may cache it. Common values:

| TTL | Meaning | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| 60-300 | 1-5 minutes | records you are about to change, failover |
| 3600 | 1 hour | typical default |
| 86400 | 1 day | stable records like NS, MX |

## Propagation explained

When you edit a record, your authoritative server answers with the new value immediately. But resolvers that cached the old answer keep using it until the old TTL runs out. Hence "it can take up to 48 hours" warnings: they assume long TTLs. With low TTLs, most of the world sees changes in minutes.

**NS changes** at the registrar (changing DNS provider) are slower, because the TLD's NS records often have TTLs of up to 2 days (for `.com`, 172800 seconds).

## Migration recipe

1. Note the current TTL (say 86400).
2. Lower it to 300.
3. **Wait** at least the old TTL (a full day here).
4. Change the record.
5. Test with several resolvers: `dig @1.1.1.1`, `dig @8.8.8.8`.
6. Keep the old target alive for a while.
7. Raise TTL back to 3600 or more.

## Negative caching

If a name does **not** exist, resolvers also cache that "no such domain" answer (NXDOMAIN) for a time set in the SOA record. If you query a name before creating it, you may need to wait a bit.

## Flushing caches locally

```bash
# Windows
ipconfig /flushdns
# macOS
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder
# Linux with systemd-resolved
resolvectl flush-caches
```

Cloudflare and Google also offer "purge cache" pages for their public resolvers.

quiz.q: A record has TTL 3600. How long can resolvers cache it?
quiz.explain: 3600 seconds is one hour.

quiz.q: What causes "DNS propagation" delays?
options: Resolvers keep cached old answers until their TTL expires
quiz.explain: It is caching, not slow transmission.

quiz.q: Before moving a site to a new server, what should you do?
options: Raise the TTL to one week
Lower the TTL in advance and wait for the old TTL to pass
quiz.explain: A low TTL makes the switch quick.

lessons.task: Run `nslookup -debug example.com` or `dig example.com` twice, a minute apart, and see the TTL count down. Then write a step-by-step plan, with times, to move `www.yoursite.com` from one server IP to another with minimal downtime.

lessons.title: Pointing a domain to your hosting
lessons.summary: Connect your domain to a website on a host using name servers or individual records.

slides.title: Two ways
slides.text:
1. **Change name servers** at the registrar to your host or DNS provider (they manage all records)
2. **Keep your DNS** and add A/AAAA/CNAME records that point to the host
slides.narration: There are two ways to connect a domain to hosting. You can change the name servers at your registrar, handing all DNS management to your host or a DNS provider. Or you can keep your current DNS and simply add records that point to the host.

slides.title: Records for a typical host
slides.text: Example: static host or PaaS
slides.narration: A typical setup looks like this. The root domain gets an A record with the IP the host gives you, or an ALIAS record. The www subdomain gets a CNAME to the platform address. Always copy the exact values from your host's dashboard.
slides.code:
# apex (root) domain
@     A      <IP from your host>
# or, if supported
@     ALIAS  myapp.hostingplatform.app.

# www
www   CNAME  myapp.hostingplatform.app.

slides.title: Add the domain at the host too
slides.text:
- In the host's dashboard: **Add custom domain**
- Host may ask for a **TXT verification** record
- Host then issues an HTTPS certificate automatically
slides.narration: DNS is only half of the job. You also need to add the custom domain in your host's dashboard, so it knows to accept traffic for that name. The host may ask you to add a TXT record to prove ownership, and will then create an HTTPS certificate for you.

slides.title: www or no www?
slides.text:
Pick one as **canonical**, redirect the other:

`example.com` -> 301 -> `www.example.com`

Good for SEO and cookies. Most hosts do this with one setting.
slides.narration: Decide whether your main address uses www or not, and redirect the other one with a permanent three oh one redirect. This avoids duplicate content in search engines. Most hosts handle this with a single setting.

slides.title: Troubleshooting
slides.text:
- `dig yoursite.com +short` shows the right IP?
- Old records conflicting (two A records)?
- TTL not expired yet?
- Cloudflare proxy (orange cloud) changes the IPs you see
- Certificate still pending? Wait, then re-check
slides.narration: If it does not work, check the basics. Does dig show the expected address? Is an old record still there, conflicting with the new one? Has the old TTL expired yet? If you use Cloudflare's proxy, you will see Cloudflare's IPs, which is normal.

lessons.notes:
## Option 1: delegate with name servers

At your registrar, replace the **NS** records with the ones your DNS provider gives you (e.g. `ana.ns.cloudflare.com`). From then on you manage all records at that provider. Good when you want a fast, feature-rich DNS (Cloudflare, Route 53, deSEC, your host's DNS).

Note: changing name servers moves **all** records. Recreate email (MX, SPF, DKIM) records first, or email will break.

## Option 2: add records

Keep DNS where it is and add:

| Name | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `@` | A | IP from host (sometimes several) |
| `@` | AAAA | IPv6 from host, if provided |
| `www` | CNAME | `yourproject.host.app.` |

Examples of typical values (always check current docs):
- **GitHub Pages**: apex A records to GitHub's four IPs (185.199.108-111.153), `www` CNAME to `username.github.io`.
- **Netlify / Vercel / Render**: `www` CNAME to the project host name; apex via A record or ALIAS/flattening.
- **Your own VPS**: A record to the server's public IP.

## Add the domain at the host

In the hosting dashboard choose **Add custom domain**. Some hosts require a **TXT verification** record (e.g. `_vercel`, `_github-pages-challenge-username`). After DNS is correct, the host issues a certificate automatically.

## Canonical host

Choose `www.example.com` or `example.com` and **301-redirect** the other. Using `www` makes CNAMEs easy and keeps cookies scoped.

## Verify

```bash
dig example.com A +short
dig www.example.com CNAME +short
curl -I https://www.example.com
```

`curl -I` shows the HTTP status and redirects.

## Common mistakes

- Leftover parking-page A records from the registrar.
- Using a CNAME at the apex where unsupported.
- Forgetting to add the domain in the host dashboard.
- Waiting on an old long TTL.

quiz.q: What happens when you change a domain's name servers?
options: A different DNS provider now answers for all the domain's records
The domain is transferred to a new owner
quiz.explain: NS delegation moves all record management to the new provider.

quiz.q: Which record is typical for pointing `www` to a hosting platform?
quiz.explain: www usually CNAMEs to the platform host name.

quiz.q: Besides DNS records, what else is usually required?
options: Adding the custom domain in the host's dashboard
quiz.explain: The host must know to serve your domain and issue a certificate.

lessons.task: Pick a static host's documentation (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages) and write out the exact DNS records you would create to serve both `example.com` and `www.example.com`, including which one redirects to the other.

lessons.title: Subdomains
lessons.summary: Organize services with subdomains like www, api, blog and app.

slides.title: Free names inside your domain
slides.text:
Own `example.com`? You can create **unlimited** subdomains for free:

- `www.example.com`
- `api.example.com`
- `blog.example.com`
- `staging.app.example.com`
slides.narration: Once you have a domain, you can create as many subdomains as you like for free, just by adding DNS records. Common ones are www, api, blog and app. They can even nest, like staging dot app dot example dot com.

slides.title: Each can point somewhere else
slides.text:
```
@        A      203.0.113.10     (VPS)
www      CNAME  mysite.netlify.app.
api      A      198.51.100.7     (backend)
blog     CNAME  hashnode.network.
status   CNAME  statuspage.provider.com.
```
slides.narration: Each subdomain can point to a different place. Your main site might be on a static host, the API on a server, the blog on a blogging platform and a status page on yet another service. All under one brand.

slides.title: Wildcards
slides.text:
`*.example.com  CNAME  app.host.com.`

- Matches any name without its own record
- Useful for multi-tenant apps: `alice.example.com`, `bob.example.com`
- Needs a wildcard certificate (DNS-01 challenge)
slides.narration: A wildcard record, written with a star, matches any subdomain that does not have its own record. It is great for apps where each customer gets their own subdomain. You will need a wildcard certificate too, which requires DNS validation.

slides.title: Subdomain vs path
slides.text:
`blog.example.com` vs `example.com/blog`

- Subdomain: separate app/host, separate cookies by default
- Path: same site, simpler SEO and cookies
slides.narration: Should you use a subdomain or a path? A subdomain is easier when the part runs on a different host or app. A path keeps everything as one site, which is simpler for search engines and cookies. Both are fine choices.

slides.title: Danger: dangling records
slides.text:
You delete the app on a host but leave `old CNAME old.herokuapp.com.`

Anyone can claim that name on the host = **subdomain takeover**.

Remove DNS records when you shut things down.
slides.narration: Watch out for dangling records. If you delete a project on a hosting platform but leave the CNAME pointing to it, an attacker might claim that name on the platform and serve their content on your subdomain. Always remove DNS records when you shut a service down.

lessons.notes:
## What is a subdomain?

Any name to the left of your registered domain is a **subdomain**. You create them by adding records in your zone; no purchase needed.

```
example.com          apex / root
www.example.com      subdomain
eu.api.example.com   nested subdomain
```

## Common patterns

| Subdomain | Typical use |
|---|---|
| `www` | main website |
| `app` | logged-in web app |
| `api` | backend API |
| `docs`, `blog`, `status` | hosted on SaaS tools |
| `staging`, `dev` | test environments |
| `mail`, `smtp` | mail servers |
| `cdn`, `static` | assets |

## Delegating a subdomain

You can even give a subdomain its own name servers:

```
dev   NS   ns1.otherprovider.net.
```

Now another team or provider controls everything under `dev.example.com`.

## Wildcards

`*.example.com` matches names that have no explicit record. It covers only one level (`a.example.com`, not `a.b.example.com`). Wildcard TLS certificates (`*.example.com`) require the **DNS-01** challenge with Let's Encrypt.

## Cookies and security

- A cookie set for `example.com` with `Domain=example.com` is sent to all subdomains, so be careful about running untrusted content on any subdomain.
- Separate apps on separate subdomains get some isolation from each other.

## Subdomain takeover

If a CNAME points to a deprovisioned resource (e.g. a deleted cloud bucket or PaaS app), an attacker can register that resource and control your subdomain. Prevent it by:
- deleting DNS records **before** or together with the resource,
- keeping an inventory of DNS records,
- periodically scanning for dangling CNAMEs.

quiz.q: How much does creating `blog.example.com` cost if you own `example.com`?
options: The same as a new domain
Nothing - just add a DNS record
It must be bought from ICANN
quiz.explain: Subdomains are free records in your own zone.

quiz.q: What does the record `*.example.com` do?
options: Matches any subdomain without its own record
quiz.explain: A wildcard catches names that have no specific record.

quiz.q: What is a subdomain takeover?
options: An attacker claiming the deleted service a dangling CNAME still points to
quiz.explain: Dangling records let attackers serve content on your name.

lessons.task: Design the subdomains for an imaginary startup with a marketing site, web app, API, docs, status page and staging environment. For each, write the record type and an example target.

lessons.title: HTTPS certificates and Let's Encrypt
lessons.summary: Secure your domain with free TLS certificates and understand how they are issued and renewed.

slides.title: Why HTTPS
slides.text:
- **Encrypts** traffic: nobody on the Wi-Fi can read it
- **Authenticates** the site: you really reached `example.com`
- Required for modern features (HTTP/2+, service workers, geolocation)
- Browsers mark HTTP as **Not secure**
slides.narration: HTTPS encrypts everything between the browser and your server, so nobody on the same network can read or change it. It also proves the browser is talking to the real site. Today it is required for many browser features, and plain HTTP is marked not secure.

slides.title: Certificates
slides.text:
A **TLS certificate** binds a domain name to a public key, signed by a **Certificate Authority (CA)** that browsers trust.

- **DV** (domain validated) - all you need for most sites
- OV / EV - add organization checks, no special browser UI today
slides.narration: A TLS certificate connects your domain name to a public key, and it is signed by a certificate authority that browsers trust. For almost every website, a domain validated certificate is all you need.

slides.title: Let's Encrypt and ACME
slides.text:
- Free, automated, non-profit CA
- Uses the **ACME** protocol
- Proves control with a challenge:
  - **HTTP-01**: file at `/.well-known/acme-challenge/`
  - **DNS-01**: TXT at `_acme-challenge` (needed for wildcards)
slides.narration: Let's Encrypt is a free, non-profit certificate authority. It uses the ACME protocol: your server proves it controls the domain, either by serving a special file over HTTP, or by creating a special TXT record in DNS. The DNS method is required for wildcard certificates.

slides.title: Getting one on a server
slides.text: With Certbot on a Linux VPS running Nginx:
slides.narration: On your own Linux server with Nginx, Certbot gets and installs a certificate in one command. It also sets up automatic renewal. Web servers like Caddy go further and handle HTTPS completely automatically.
slides.code:
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com

# test automatic renewal
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

slides.title: Short lifetimes: automate!
slides.text:
- Let's Encrypt certificates last **90 days** (shorter options are rolling out)
- Industry max lifetime is shrinking: **200 days** from March 2026, heading to **47 days** by 2029
- Manual renewal is no longer realistic
- Most hosts (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare, Render) renew for you
slides.narration: Certificates are getting shorter lived. Let's Encrypt certificates last ninety days, and the industry wide maximum dropped to two hundred days in March twenty twenty six, with a plan to reach forty seven days by twenty twenty nine. That means renewal must be automatic. Most hosting platforms already do this for you.

slides.title: Extra hardening
slides.text:
- Redirect HTTP -> HTTPS (301)
- **HSTS** header: browsers only use HTTPS
- **CAA** record: only allow your CA
- Use TLS 1.2+ (TLS 1.3 preferred)
slides.narration: A few extra steps make HTTPS stronger. Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS, send the HSTS header so browsers never use plain HTTP again, add a CAA record that lists which authorities may issue certificates for you, and only allow modern TLS versions.

lessons.notes:
## TLS in one paragraph

**HTTPS** is HTTP over **TLS**. During the TLS handshake the server presents a **certificate** proving it owns the domain; browser and server agree on keys; then all traffic is encrypted and integrity-protected. TLS 1.3 is the modern default.

## Certificate types

- **DV** - Domain Validated: proves control of the domain. Free from Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services.
- **OV/EV** - add organization identity checks; browsers no longer show special indicators, so most sites use DV.
- **Wildcard** - `*.example.com`, requires DNS-01 validation.
- **SAN / multi-domain** - one certificate for several names.

## ACME and Let's Encrypt

**ACME** (RFC 8555) automates issuance and renewal. Clients: **Certbot**, **acme.sh**, **lego**, and built-in support in **Caddy**, Traefik and many hosts.

Challenges:
- **HTTP-01** - the CA fetches `http://example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>`.
- **DNS-01** - you publish a TXT record `_acme-challenge.example.com`.
- **TLS-ALPN-01** - proof over port 443.

```bash
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
```

## Lifetimes are shrinking

- Let's Encrypt certificates are valid **90 days** and the CA is moving towards shorter, optional 6-day and 45-day certificates.
- The CA/Browser Forum reduced the maximum lifetime for all public certificates to **200 days from 15 March 2026**, then 100 days (2027) and **47 days (2029)**.
- Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry reminder emails in 2025, so **monitor** your certificates and make renewal automatic.

## Hardening checklist

- 301 redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
- `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`.
- `CAA` record: `example.com. CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"`.
- Disable TLS 1.0/1.1. Test with SSL Labs.

On managed hosts (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare, GitHub Pages, Render), certificates are issued and renewed automatically once DNS points correctly.

quiz.q: Which challenge type is required for a wildcard certificate from Let's Encrypt?
quiz.explain: Wildcards require proving control via a DNS TXT record.

quiz.q: Why must certificate renewal be automated today?
options: Lifetimes are short (90 days and shrinking) so manual renewal is error-prone
quiz.explain: Short lifetimes make automation essential.

quiz.q: What does the HSTS header do?
options: Tells browsers to only use HTTPS for the site
quiz.explain: HSTS forces HTTPS for future visits.

lessons.task: Open three websites and click the lock icon in your browser. For each, note the certificate issuer (CA), the validity dates and how many days the certificate lasts in total. Then look up their CAA records with `dig example.com CAA` or `nslookup -type=CAA example.com`.

lessons.title: Email records: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
lessons.summary: Set up DNS records so your domain's email is delivered and cannot be easily spoofed.

slides.title: Email trusts too easily
slides.text:
Old SMTP lets anyone write `From: boss@yourcompany.com`.

Three DNS-based checks fix this:
- **SPF** - who may send
- **DKIM** - signature on each message
- **DMARC** - policy + reports
slides.narration: Email was designed long ago, and the basic protocol lets anyone put any address in the From line. Three DNS based standards fix this. SPF lists who may send, DKIM signs each message, and DMARC ties them together with a policy.

slides.title: SPF
slides.text:
A TXT record listing allowed senders:

`v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all`

- Only **one** SPF record per domain
- Max **10 DNS lookups**
- `-all` fail, `~all` softfail
slides.narration: SPF is a TXT record listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain, often by including your email provider. You may only have one SPF record, and it may trigger at most ten DNS lookups. The ending says what to do with others: dash all means fail, tilde all means soft fail.

slides.title: DKIM
slides.text:
Your mail server **signs** each message with a private key.

Public key published in DNS:

`selector1._domainkey.example.com  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIB..."`

Receivers verify the signature.
slides.narration: DKIM adds a digital signature to each message. Your email provider signs messages with a private key, and you publish the matching public key in a TXT record under a selector name and underscore domainkey. Receivers check the signature to make sure the message really came from you and was not changed.

slides.title: DMARC
slides.text:
`_dmarc.example.com TXT "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"`

- Requires SPF or DKIM to pass **and align** with the From domain
- `p=none` -> monitor, `quarantine` -> spam, `reject` -> block
- `rua` = aggregate reports
slides.narration: DMARC tells receivers what to do when a message fails. It requires SPF or DKIM to pass, and the domain to match the visible From address. The policy can be none for monitoring, quarantine to send failures to spam, or reject to block them. Reports are emailed to the rua address.

slides.title: Roll out safely
slides.text:
1. Set up SPF and DKIM for **every** service that sends as you
2. Start DMARC with `p=none`, read reports
3. Fix missing senders
4. Move to `p=quarantine`, then `p=reject`
slides.narration: Roll this out step by step. First set up SPF and DKIM for every service that sends email as you, including newsletters and invoices. Start DMARC with p equals none and read the reports. When all legitimate mail passes, move to quarantine and finally reject.

slides.title: Why it matters in 2026
slides.text:
- Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft Outlook **require** SPF, DKIM and DMARC for bulk senders
- Missing records = mail in spam or rejected
- Also: MX records, reverse DNS (PTR), and a one-click unsubscribe for marketing mail
slides.narration: This is not optional anymore. Gmail and Yahoo started requiring SPF, DKIM and DMARC for bulk senders in twenty twenty four, and Microsoft Outlook followed in twenty twenty five. Without these records, your mail goes to spam or is rejected.

lessons.notes:
## The problem

SMTP does not verify the `From:` address. Spammers and phishers exploit this. Three DNS-published standards let receivers check mail.

## MX first

To **receive** email you need MX records from your provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Zoho, Proton, Fastmail...).

## SPF (Sender Policy Framework)

A single TXT record at the domain:

```
example.com.  TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:mailgun.org -all"
```

- Mechanisms: `ip4:`, `ip6:`, `a`, `mx`, `include:`.
- Qualifiers: `-all` (fail), `~all` (softfail), `?all` (neutral). Never `+all`.
- Limit: 10 DNS lookups; exactly one SPF record.
- SPF checks the hidden envelope sender (Return-Path), not the visible From.

## DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)

The sending service signs headers and body. You publish the public key at `<selector>._domainkey.example.com` (often given as a CNAME by your provider). Use 2048-bit keys and rotate them occasionally.

## DMARC

```
_dmarc.example.com.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com; adkim=r; aspf=r"
```

- Passes if SPF **or** DKIM passes **and aligns** with the visible From domain.
- `p=none` -> monitor; `p=quarantine` -> spam folder; `p=reject` -> refuse.
- `rua` -> daily aggregate XML reports (use a free DMARC report viewer).

## Requirements

Since 2024 Gmail and Yahoo, and since 2025 Microsoft for Outlook.com, require bulk senders (around 5,000+ messages/day) to have SPF, DKIM and DMARC (at least `p=none`), aligned From domains, low spam rates and one-click unsubscribe. All senders need at least SPF or DKIM.

## Domains that never send email

Protect them from spoofing:

```
@       TXT  "v=spf1 -all"
_dmarc  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=reject;"
```

## Bonus

- **MTA-STS** and **TLS-RPT**: require encrypted delivery to your servers.
- **BIMI**: shows your logo in some inboxes (needs DMARC enforcement).

quiz.q: Which record lists the servers allowed to send email for your domain?
quiz.explain: SPF is a TXT record listing authorized senders.

quiz.q: Where is a DMARC policy published?
options: At the apex as an MX
quiz.explain: DMARC lives at _dmarc.example.com as TXT.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to start DMARC?
quiz.explain: Monitor first to avoid blocking legitimate mail.

lessons.task: Look up the email records of a big domain: `nslookup -type=TXT gmail.com`, `nslookup -type=TXT _dmarc.google.com` and `nslookup -type=MX google.com`. Explain each part. Then write the SPF, DKIM (placeholder key) and DMARC records for a domain that sends mail through one provider of your choice.
